title: Three posts, three looks
scenario:
You make a week of social posts for a café called Moss & Mill. The client's look is a flat, friendly illustration in cream, forest green and terracotta.

You wrote each prompt on its own. Post 1 looks right. Posts 2 and 3 look like they come from other brands. The exhibit shows the three prompts and what came back.
exhibit:
Prompt 1
  "A flat vector illustration with bold clean outlines of a hand holding a green cup, cream background, forest green and terracotta."
  -> flat, outlined, cream background. Matches the brand.

Prompt 2
  "A cozy croissant on a plate, warm cafe vibes, nice colours."
  -> glossy photo style, brown tones, wooden table.

Prompt 3
  "A cute coffee machine, modern look."
  -> 3D render, grey and chrome, dark background.

Client note
  "We will post one image a day for 14 days. They must look like one family."

questions.prompt: What is the main reason the three images look different?

options.text: The model is random, so no prompt can fix it, whatever you write.
options.explanation: Randomness exists, but the exhibit shows a clear cause: only prompt 1 names a medium, outlines and a palette.

options.text: Prompts 2 and 3 describe no style, so the model picked a look.
options.explanation: Right. "Cozy", "nice colours" and "modern look" give no medium, line, colour or background. The model fills the gaps differently each time.

options.text: Croissants and coffee machines can only be drawn as photos or 3D.
options.explanation: Any subject can be drawn in a flat vector style. Prompt 1 shows that.

options.text: Prompt 1 was too short, so the model drew it in the wrong style.
options.explanation: Prompt 1 is the one that worked. It named the medium, the outlines, the colours and the background.

questions.prompt: Which change gives you 14 matching images with the least risk?

options.text: Write one style block and put it at the top of every prompt. Change only the subject.
options.explanation: Right. Google's stylised-image template separates the style from the subject, and this keeps the style words identical in every prompt.

options.text: Add the word "consistent" to the start and the end of every prompt, in capital letters.
options.explanation: The word names no medium, colour or line. It gives the model nothing to repeat.

options.text: Write a brand-new, longer style description for each post, to be safe and fresh.
options.explanation: New wording each time brings back the problem. The style words must be the same across posts.

options.text: Use prompt 1's style for post 1 only and let the other posts find their own look.
options.explanation: The client wants one family of images across 14 days.

questions.prompt: You send 4 of the client's old posts to Claude and ask it to describe their shared style. It says: "hand-painted watercolour, soft edges". You can see the posts are flat vector with sharp outlines. What do you do?

options.text: Paste its description into the style block. It looked at the real images, so it must be right.
options.explanation: Anthropic's docs say Claude might hallucinate or make mistakes and that you should carefully review its image interpretations.

options.text: Correct the description yourself (flat vector, sharp outlines) and use it as your draft.
options.explanation: Right. The vision model gives a first draft. You know the client's work and you fix the errors.

options.text: Stop using vision models for style work. They cannot read images, so the answer was a guess.
options.explanation: They can read images. They can also be wrong, so you review the answer.

options.text: Run the same request ten times and use the most common answer in your style block.
options.explanation: Repeating a request does not make a wrong reading right. You can see the posts and can correct the text in one minute.

questions.prompt: On day 9 one image has a slightly different green and softer lines. What is the best habit?

options.text: Compare each new image to an approved anchor before posting, and fix any that drift.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's docs say consistency across generations is a known limit, so you check each one against a fixed example (the anchor is our habit).

options.text: Ignore it. Nobody will notice a small colour change in one image out of 14 posts.
options.explanation: A client who asked for one family will notice. Small drifts add up over 14 posts.

options.text: Rewrite the whole style block every time a drift appears in any new image.
options.explanation: Changing the block each time creates more differences. Freeze the block and check against the anchor.

options.text: Stop the campaign and start again with a new brand look and a new anchor image.
options.explanation: One drifting image is a review point, not a reason to drop the brand look.
